options.text: All cycloalkanes have identical ring strain.

options.label: B
options.text: Cyclohexane (0 kJ/mol) < Cyclopentane (27 kJ/mol) < Cyclobutane (110 kJ/mol) < Cyclopropane (115 kJ/mol) in Chapter 27.

questions.correct_answer: Cyclohexane (0 kJ/mol) < Cyclopentane (27 kJ/mol) < Cyclobutane (110 kJ/mol) < Cyclopropane (115 kJ/mol) in Chapter 27.
questions.explanation: Ring strain is maximized in small 3- and 4-membered rings due to severe angle distortion and eclipsing torsional strain.

questions.question: Rank the principal acidic functional groups encountered in Chapter 27 in order of increasing acidity (lowest to highest pKa):

options.label: A
options.text: Alkanes (pKa ~50) < Amines (pKa ~38) < Terminal Alkynes (pKa ~25) < Alcohols (pKa ~16) < Phenols (pKa ~10) < Carboxylic acids (pKa ~4.8) in Chapter 27.

options.label: B
options.text: Carboxylic acids < Phenols < Alcohols < Alkynes < Amines.

questions.correct_answer: Alkanes (pKa ~50) < Amines (pKa ~38) < Terminal Alkynes (pKa ~25) < Alcohols (pKa ~16) < Phenols (pKa ~10) < Carboxylic acids (pKa ~4.8) in Chapter 27.
questions.explanation: Brønsted acidity follows the universal pKa hierarchy dictated by ARIO conjugate base stabilization rules.

questions.question: Rank the intermediate carbocations in Chapter 27 in order of increasing thermodynamic stability:

options.label: C
options.text: Methyl cation < Primary (1°) < Secondary (2°) < Tertiary (3°) < Allylic/Benzylic < Oxocarbenium ion [R-C⁺=O ↔ R-C≡O⁺] in Chapter 27.

questions.correct_answer: Methyl cation < Primary (1°) < Secondary (2°) < Tertiary (3°) < Allylic/Benzylic < Oxocarbenium ion [R-C⁺=O ↔ R-C≡O⁺] in Chapter 27.
questions.explanation: Carbocation stability increases with hyperconjugation, resonance delocalization, and octet-complete lone-pair donation.

questions.question: Rank the common leaving groups in Chapter 27 in order of increasing leaving group ability (worst to best):

options.label: B
options.text: Hydroxide (OH⁻) < Fluoride (F⁻) < Chloride (Cl⁻) < Bromide (Br⁻) < Iodide (I⁻) ≈ Tosylate (OTs⁻) in Chapter 27.

questions.correct_answer: Hydroxide (OH⁻) < Fluoride (F⁻) < Chloride (Cl⁻) < Bromide (Br⁻) < Iodide (I⁻) ≈ Tosylate (OTs⁻) in Chapter 27.
questions.explanation: Leaving group ability correlates inversely with basicity: the conjugate bases of strong acids (low pKa) are the best leaving groups.

questions.topic: Ch27 Nucleophilicity Ranking in Polar Aprotic Solvent
questions.question: Rank the halide nucleophiles in order of increasing nucleophilicity in DMSO/DMF (polar aprotic solvent) for Chapter 27:

options.label: B
options.text: I⁻ < Br⁻ < Cl⁻ < F⁻ in polar aprotic solvents (inverting the protic solvent trend) in Chapter 27.

options.label: D
options.text: F⁻ < Cl⁻ < Br⁻ < I⁻ in polar aprotic solvents.

questions.correct_answer: I⁻ < Br⁻ < Cl⁻ < F⁻ in polar aprotic solvents (inverting the protic solvent trend) in Chapter 27.
questions.explanation: In aprotic solvents without hydrogen bonding, basicity dictates nucleophilicity: compact, electron-dense F⁻ is the strongest nucleophile.

questions.topic: Ch27 Boiling Point Molecular Structure Ranking
questions.question: Rank the constitutional isomers of Chapter 27 organic targets in order of increasing boiling point:

options.label: A
options.text: All isomers have identical boiling points.

options.label: D
options.text: Highly branched isomers < Moderately branched isomers < Linear straight-chain isomers < Hydrogen-bonding derivatives in Chapter 27.

questions.correct_answer: Highly branched isomers < Moderately branched isomers < Linear straight-chain isomers < Hydrogen-bonding derivatives in Chapter 27.
questions.explanation: Boiling points increase with greater molecular surface contact area (London dispersion) and stronger intermolecular hydrogen bonding.

questions.question: Rank the carbonyl functional groups in Chapter 27 in order of increasing electrophilicity toward nucleophiles:

options.label: A
options.text: Amide < Ester < Ketone < Aldehyde < Acyl Chloride in Chapter 27.

options.label: B
options.text: Aldehyde < Ketone < Amide < Ester < Acyl Chloride.

options.label: C
options.text: Acyl Chloride < Aldehyde < Ketone < Ester < Amide.

options.label: D
options.text: Ketone < Aldehyde < Ester < Amide < Acyl Chloride.

questions.correct_answer: Amide < Ester < Ketone < Aldehyde < Acyl Chloride in Chapter 27.
questions.explanation: Carbonyl electrophilicity decreases with resonance electron donation from heteroatoms and increases with electron withdrawal by halogens.

questions.question: Rank the carbon radical intermediates in Chapter 27 in order of increasing stability:

options.label: D
options.text: Methyl radical (•CH₃) < Primary (1°) < Secondary (2°) < Tertiary (3°) < Allylic < Benzylic radical in Chapter 27.

questions.correct_answer: Methyl radical (•CH₃) < Primary (1°) < Secondary (2°) < Tertiary (3°) < Allylic < Benzylic radical in Chapter 27.
questions.explanation: Carbon radicals are electron-deficient (7 valence electrons) and are stabilized by hyperconjugation and π-resonance delocalization.

questions.question: Rank the alkenes of Chapter 27 in order of increasing thermodynamic stability (lowest to highest heat of combustion):

options.label: B
options.text: Monosubstituted < Disubstituted (cis < trans) < Trisubstituted < Tetrasubstituted alkene in Chapter 27.

questions.correct_answer: Monosubstituted < Disubstituted (cis < trans) < Trisubstituted < Tetrasubstituted alkene in Chapter 27.
questions.explanation: Each alkyl substituent stabilizes the alkene π bond by ~10–12 kJ/mol via hyperconjugative orbital overlap.
